## The Founding of the New Zealand Labour Party

The New Zealand Labour Party wasn't founded by a single individual — it emerged from a collective effort by left-wing organisations and trade unions. In July 1916, in Wellington, representatives of these groups — including several members of Parliament — resolved that 'the time has arrived for the formation of a New Zealand Labour Party for the purpose of consolidating the political forces of Labour'. [[1]](cite://1/1)

The party was essentially the political wing of the union movement, set up and financed by trade unions that had grown significantly alongside New Zealand's expanding industrial cities in the early 20th century. [[2]](cite://2/1)

### Key Figures Involved in the Founding

While no single founder is credited, several individuals played notable roles in establishing the party:

- **James McCombs** helped draft the party's constitution and programme, and served as its first president — though he resigned a year later over the party's approach to prohibition. [[3]](cite://3/1)
- **Michael Joseph Savage** supported the formation of the united Labour Party in July 1916, becoming its national vice president in 1918 and its first permanent national secretary in 1919. [[4]](cite://4/1)
- **John Kendrick Archer** was an active advocate for the party's formation prior to 1916, and the Social Democratic Party he had joined was absorbed into the Labour Party that year. [[5]](cite://5/1)

### Roots in the Union Movement

The founding ideology was strongly influenced by Marxist and syndicalist ideas, with Labour's 1916 policy objective calling for 'the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange' — meaning state ownership and control of major parts of the economy. [[2]](cite://2/2) The trade union movement had already been flexing its muscles through events like the 1890 maritime strike and the Waikato and waterside strikes of 1912–13, and setbacks on the industrial front turned the labour movement towards political action. [[6]](cite://6/1)

Note also that there was an earlier forerunner: the Political Labour League of New Zealand, described as the country's first independent labour party, was formed in 1904 — though this was a separate entity from the 1916 Labour Party. [[7]](cite://7/1)

Founded by left-wing organisations and trade unions, the party evolved from a union-based socialist movement to a broad-based social democratic party. The Labour Party achieved significant electoral success in 1935, winning 53 of 80 seats and forming the first Labour government (1935-1949), which introduced major social reforms including state housing, free health services, and government control of banks and broadcasting. Subsequent Labour governments served in 1957-60, 1972-75, 1984-90, 1999-2008, and 2017-2023. The 1984 Labour government under David Lange dramatically shifted toward neo-liberalism and "Rogernomics," privatizing state assets. Later governments under Helen Clark (1999-2008) and Jacinda Ardern (2017-23) retreated from neo-liberalism and governed under proportional representation and coalition arrangements. The party abandoned its explicit socialist objective in 1951, adopting social democratic principles. By the early 21st century, Labour evolved into a "catch-all" party drawing support across occupational, ethnic, gender, and educational groups. Women have been integral to the party since its inception, with notable figures including Elizabeth McCombs, Mabel Howard, Helen Clark, and Jacinda Ardern as prime ministers. The document outlines the party's organisational structure, including local branches, 11 affiliated unions, 72 electorate committees, six geographic regions, and national bodies for candidate selection and policy development.

[Page 1] Early years of the party The Labour Party was founded as a workers’ party in 1916 by left wing organisations and trade unions. From early on there was tension between members who were more moderate and those who were militantly against capitalism. In the 1919 election the new party did very well, gaining 24% of the vote. First Labour government In the 1935 election the Labour Party won 53 of the 80 seats and became the government. In response to the economic depression of the time, the Labour government introduced wide reaching programmes, including: building state houses introducing free health services for everyone bringing banks and broadcasting under government control. The government and its policies were popular enough to stay in power until 1949. The ideas of reforming society within capitalism and the importance of the welfare state remained core Labour Party policies for most of the 20th century. Second and third Labour governments The second (1957 60) and third (1972 75) Labour governments only stayed in power for one term each. In 1974 the popular Labour Prime Minister Norman Kirk died suddenly, and that, combined with an economic downturn, led to a loss of support for the government. Fourth Labour government The Labour government elected in 1984 was very different from previous ones. Most of its members of Parliament were lawyers or academics, rather than workers or trade unionists. It also had very different economic policies, privatised state assets, and reduced the role of the government in the economy. It was often at odds with traditional Labour Party beliefs. It was voted out in 1990. Fifth and sixth Labour governments The 1999 2008 Labour government returned to more traditional Labour policies. It was led by Helen Clark, New Zealand’s first woman prime minister to take office following an election. It was the first Labour government under the mixed member proportional representation (MMP) system and, because it didn’t have a clear majority, it needed support from other parties to govern. In 2017 Labour, led by Jacinda Ardern, returned to power in a coalition with New Zealand First that was supported by the Green Party. In 2020 Labour received enough votes to govern alone, but chose to offer ministerial positions outside cabinet to the two Green Party co leaders. In 2023 the Labour government was defeated. Māori and the Labour Party From the 1930s there was a strong tie between Labour and Māori, and for most of the rest of the 20th century Labour won all the Māori seats. The party began to lose support from Māori in the 1980s and other parties, including the Māori Party (later Te Pāti Māori), began to win Māori seats. Labour won back all seven Māori seats in 2017, but Te Pāti Māori regained two in 2020 and six in 2023. Women and the Labour Party Women were involved with the party from the beginning. The first woman MP was Labour MP Elizabeth McCombs, and Mabel Howard was the first woman cabinet minister. The party has a women’s council, and women are guaranteed places on decision making groups. Organisation of the party Members of the Labour Party either belong to a local branch or to a union that is affiliated to the Labour Party. Each electorate has a committee, and there is a national council.

[Page 10] In the first decades of the 20th century, industries grew strongly in New Zealand’s main cities and union membership also increased. The Labour Party was formed in this period as the political wing of the union movement, and was set up and financed by trade unions. The party’s members were mostly the members of unions affiliated to the party (known as affiliate members). Individual members belonging to local party branches (general members) were at first a minority. Widening appeal To become a governing party, Labour had to widen its appeal to include other sections of the population. [Page 3] The New Zealand Labour Party was formed in 1916, just months before the introduction of conscription for the First World War. The party firmly opposed conscription and several of its leaders, including Peter Fraser, Bob Semple and Harry Holland, were arrested for sedition. Paddy Webb, the MP for West Coast, lost his seat due to his anti conscription stance and went to jail, but was re elected while serving his sentence. However, Fraser, Semple and Webb were all ministers in the government that brought in conscription during the Second World War.

[Page 1] Formation and rise The National Party was set up in 1936, when the two main conservative parties, Reform and United, merged. The two parties had campaigned together as the National Political Federation in the 1935 election, but lost to Labour in a landslide. Sidney Holland led National to win for the first time, in the 1949 election. He believed in individual freedom and responsibility, and was tough on watersiders during the 1951 waterfront labour dispute. Holland was replaced by Keith Holyoake in 1957. Labour won in 1957, but National then won four elections in a row. 1960s to 1980s National was in power through the 1960s. It was a decade of rising prosperity for most New Zealanders, but from 1965 there were also protests for women’s rights and the environment, and against the Vietnam War. Robert Muldoon became National’s leader in 1974, and prime minister the following year. He was popular at first, but was later in conflict with both liberals and conservatives. His government regulated the economy strongly. When National MP Marilyn Waring decided to vote for Labour’s nuclear free legislation in 1984, Muldoon called a snap election which Labour won in a landslide. 1980s to 2020s National, led by Jim Bolger, won the election in 1990. Bolger’s government continued the economic reforms of the previous Labour government. They cut welfare benefits, and passed laws to make union membership voluntary. In 1996 MMP (mixed member proportional representation) was introduced, and National formed a coalition government with the New Zealand First party. In 1997 Bolger was ousted as leader by Jenny Shipley, New Zealand’s first woman prime minister. However, the next three elections resulted in Labour led governments. In 2008 John Key led National to victory, forming a government with support from the Māori Party, ACT and UnitedFuture. Bill English succeeded Key as prime minister and party leader in 2016, but National lost power to Labour after the 2017 election and was heavily defeated in 2020. In 2023, under Christopher Luxon, National was able to form a coalition government with ACT and New Zealand First. Party organisation In the early 1970s National had about 200,000 members, from many different parts of society. However, party membership later declined. National’s party organisation, which is separate from its parliamentary section, holds an annual conference to elect its governing board, hear from senior MPs and, in closed sessions, discuss policies. While some Māori leaders have been involved with National, the party has never had broad support among Māori. However, the 2008 17 National led government was supported by the Māori Party (Te Pāti Māori). The National Party is New Zealand’s most successful political party. By 2023 it had been in government for 47 of its 87 years in existence, a longer tenure than any other party.

21.document_title: James Thorn: A Biography of New Zealand Labour Pioneer
21.document_summary: James Thorn (1882-1956) was a prominent New Zealand labour activist and politician. Born in Christchurch to a butcher's family, Thorn initially worked as a moulder before serving in South Africa, where witnessing civilian casualties transformed him into a pacifist. Influenced by labour advocate Jack McCullough, he became deeply involved in labour organizing, serving as secretary of the metalworkers' union and helping organize agricultural labourers in Canterbury. He stood for Parliament in 1905 and 1908 with the Political Labour League before spending four years in Britain as a socialist propagandist. Arrested for anti-conscription activism during WWI, Thorn married Margaret Anderson in 1917 and spent the 1920s as editor of the Maoriland Worker and Labour Party official. He finally won parliamentary election in 1935 as member for Thames, serving 11 years with particular interest in collective security and the United Nations. After losing his seat in 1946, he served as High Commissioner to Canada and participated in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. He died in 1956.

22.document_title: William Ferguson Massey: Life, Political Career, and Legacy as Prime Minister of New Zealand
22.document_summary: William Ferguson Massey (1856-1925) was a transformative figure in New Zealand politics who rose from humble beginnings as a farmer in Māngere to become Prime Minister from 1912 to 1925. Born in Northern Ireland and migrating to New Zealand in 1870, Massey entered Parliament in 1894 and became opposition leader in 1903. He led the Reform Party to victory in 1911 and formed a cabinet of nine members. As Prime Minister, Massey navigated major industrial disputes including the 1912 Waihī miners' strike and 1913 waterfront strikes, employing controversial "Massey's Cossacks" special constables. During World War I, he formed a coalition government with the Liberals in 1915 and represented New Zealand at the Paris Peace Conference, signing the Treaty of Versailles in 1919. His 1919 election victory provided his only clear parliamentary majority. Between 1923-1925, he implemented economic reforms including pension increases and agricultural support. Despite his public rustic persona, Massey demonstrated exceptional parliamentary skill and political acumen, transforming opposition into an organized political party. He died of cancer on 10 May 1925, leaving a legacy of 31 years in Parliament.

24.document_title: Michael Joseph Savage: Life, Political Career, and Legacy as New Zealand's Social Security Pioneer
24.document_summary: Michael Joseph Savage (1872-1940) was an Irish-Australian-born New Zealand Labour politician who became the nation's first Labour Prime Minister. Born in Victoria, Australia, Savage emigrated to New Zealand in 1907 and became active in unionism and socialist movements in Auckland. Elected to Parliament in 1919 representing Auckland West, he became Labour leader in 1933. His advocacy for pensions, free healthcare, and workers' rights resonated during the Great Depression. Labour won the 1935 election with 55 of 80 seats, implementing progressive legislation including state house construction and Reserve Bank nationalization. At the 1937 Imperial Conference, Savage criticized Britain's appeasement policies. In 1938, despite terminal colon cancer, he championed the Social Security Bill, introducing universal free healthcare and pensions termed "applied Christianity." Labour's vote share increased from 46% to 56%. Savage died on March 27, 1940, leaving a legacy that fundamentally shaped New Zealand's social welfare system for generations.

25.document_title: Ernest John Bartlett Allen: A Biography
25.document_summary: Ernest John Bartlett Allen (1884-1945) was a British-born socialist activist and intellectual who became a leading figure in industrial unionism and revolutionary socialism. Born in Berkshire, he studied European languages at Oxford and joined the Social Democratic Federation before moving to the Socialist Labour Party, where he championed industrial unionism as the path to revolution. He founded the Advocates of Industrial Unionism and edited the Industrialist, publishing influential works on revolutionary tactics. In 1910, he joined Tom Mann's Industrial Syndicalist Education League. Relocating to New Zealand in 1912, Allen became assistant editor of the Māoriland Worker and later its editor. Initially supporting WWI and conscription, he lost his position but continued writing on socialist strategy. 29.document_title: Richard John Seddon: Life, Political Rise, Leadership, and Legacy as New Zealand's Premier
29.document_summary: This comprehensive biographical account traces Richard John Seddon's life from his birth in Lancashire, England in 1845 through his rise to prominence as New Zealand's Premier. Beginning as an unruly student interested in mechanical drawing, Seddon was apprenticed as an engineer and eventually emigrated to New Zealand in 1863, where he prospected for gold and worked at railway workshops. After settling on the West Coast and establishing businesses including a hotel and store at Kūmara, he married Louisa Spotswood in 1869 and became a miners' advocate and local politician. Elected to Parliament in 1879 for Hokitika, he represented mining constituencies and became known for his focus on West Coast issues. By the late 1880s, he had risen to prominence as a leading mining authority and opposition figure. Seddon became Premier in 1893, outmaneuvering rival Robert Stout following John Ballance's death. His populist style and mastery of parliamentary procedure enabled him to centralize power, earning the nickname "King Dick" for his autocratic governance. As Premier, he held multiple portfolios including labour, colonial treasurer, education, and immigration, implementing key reforms such as the Old-age Pensions Act 1898, Industrial Conciliation and Arbitration Act 1894, and Workers' Dwellings Act 1905. Known for his imposing physical presence and carefully cultivated public image, Seddon excelled at crowd management and maintaining public sympathy while consolidating Liberal reforms. He pursued imperialist expansion in the Pacific, notably annexing the Cook Islands in 1901, and maintained strict party discipline. His health declined from 1897 onwards, yet he remained in power until his death on June 10, 1906, aboard the Oswestry Grange while returning from Australia. His legacy encompasses humanitarianism, imperialism, and populist prime-ministerial leadership in New Zealand.

30.document_summary: William Arthur Moffatt (Māwhete), born 1880 in Tiakitahuna, was a prominent Māori political leader and advocate of Ngāti Hineaute descent with connections to multiple iwi. Working as an interpreter and land agent before entering politics, Māwhete stood unsuccessfully for the Western Māori seat in 1914 and 1922, then became the Labour Party's candidate in 1925, losing to Māui Pōmare. Appointed to the Legislative Council in 1936, he served until 1950 as the sole Māori member, championing Treaty of Waitangi rights, Māori welfare, and equal treatment. Founded by left-wing organisations and trade unions, the party evolved from a union-based socialist movement to a broad-based social democratic party. Subsequent Labour governments served in 1957-60, 1972-75, 1984-90, 1999-2008, and 2017-2023. The 1984 Labour government under David Lange dramatically shifted toward neo-liberalism and "Rogernomics," privatizing state assets. Later governments under Helen Clark (1999-2008) and Jacinda Ardern (2017-23) retreated from neo-liberalism and governed under proportional representation and coalition arrangements. The party abandoned its explicit socialist objective in 1951, adopting social democratic principles. By the early 21st century, Labour evolved into a "catch-all" party drawing support across occupational, ethnic, gender, and educational groups. Women have been integral to the party since its inception, with notable figures including Elizabeth McCombs, Mabel Howard, Helen Clark, and Jacinda Ardern as prime ministers. chunkHighlights.text: In the first decades of the 20th century, industries grew strongly in New Zealand’s main cities and union membership also increased. The Labour Party was formed in this period as the political wing of the union movement, and was set up and financed by trade unions. Many union leaders adopted the ideas of Marxists and syndicalists, which had the revolutionary aim of overthrowing capitalism and abolishing the

wage-earning system. Their aims were expressed in Labour’s 1916 policy objective, which called for ‘the socialisation of the means of production, distribution and exchange’. 1 This meant state ownership and control of all major parts of the economy.

Labour therefore began as a narrowly based sectional party. Its founding focus was on the needs of wage workers, who soon guaranteed the party a secure base in the poorer urban, milling and mining electorates. The party’s members were mostly the members of unions affiliated to the party (known as affiliate members). Individual members belonging to local party branches (general members) were at first a minority.

To become a governing party, Labour had to widen its appeal to include other sections of the population. It began to do this in the 1920s and 1930s by shaping its policies to the specific problems of those times. The poverty and insecurity that spread through the community during the depression years made this transition easier.

4.fileDescription: Michael Joseph Savage (1872-1940) was an Irish-Australian-born New Zealand Labour politician who became the nation's first Labour Prime Minister. Born in Victoria, Australia, Savage emigrated to New Zealand in 1907 and became active in unionism and socialist movements in Auckland. Elected to Parliament in 1919 representing Auckland West, he became Labour leader in 1933. His advocacy for pensions, free healthcare, and workers' rights resonated during the Great Depression. Labour won the 1935 election with 55 of 80 seats, implementing progressive legislation including state house construction and Reserve Bank nationalization. At the 1937 Imperial Conference, Savage criticized Britain's appeasement policies. In 1938, despite terminal colon cancer, he championed the Social Security Bill, introducing universal free healthcare and pensions termed "applied Christianity." Labour's vote share increased from 46% to 56%. Savage died on March 27, 1940, leaving a legacy that fundamentally shaped New Zealand's social welfare system for generations.

5.fileDescription: John Kendrick Archer (1865-1949) was a prominent Baptist minister and New Zealand Labour Party leader. Born in Leicestershire, England, he was ordained in 1891 and served as a pastor in northern England before immigrating to New Zealand in 1908. Influenced by Baptist preacher John Clifford and committed to Christian socialism, Archer became a powerful advocate for social justice and workers' rights. In New Zealand, he held significant positions including president of the Baptist Union (1916-1918), mayor of Christchurch (1925-1931), and Labour Party president (1928-1929). Though unsuccessful in four parliamentary campaigns, he was appointed to the Legislative Council in 1937. Archer was known for his uncompromising moral stance, blending religious conviction with political activism, and remained active in church and community work until his death.

6.fileDescription: This comprehensive document traces New Zealand's historical trajectory from Māori settlement around 1250-1300 CE through the early 21st century. It covers Polynesian settlement and tribal societies, European discovery by Abel Tasman (1642) and James Cook (1769-70), and early European interaction through sealers, whalers, and traders. From 1814, missionaries introduced Christianity and European farming techniques. The Treaty of Waitangi (1840) established British sovereignty while guaranteeing Māori rights, though interpretation differences complicated implementation. European settlement escalated through the New Zealand Company, the 1852 Constitution Act, and land conflicts resulting in the Taranaki Wars and Waikato campaign with large-scale land confiscation. Economic development progressed through wool production, gold discoveries, Julius Vogel's public works program, and the frozen-meat industry. Politically, the Liberal Party's 1890 victory established a "family farm" economy, women's suffrage followed in 1893, and the First World War established the Anzac tradition. Labour's 1935 victory under Michael Joseph Savage introduced welfare reforms, while Labour's 1984 economic liberalization transformed the nation. From the 1970s onwards, New Zealand underwent bicultural and multicultural transformation, highlighted by the 1981 Springbok rugby tour, the Waitangi Tribunal's establishment (1975), Māori cultural renaissance and language revitalization, and the emergence of significant Pasifika and Asian populations.

7.fileDescription: James Thorn (1882-1956) was a prominent New Zealand labour activist and politician. Born in Christchurch to a butcher's family, Thorn initially worked as a moulder before serving in South Africa, where witnessing civilian casualties transformed him into a pacifist. Influenced by labour advocate Jack McCullough, he became deeply involved in labour organizing, serving as secretary of the metalworkers' union and helping organize agricultural labourers in Canterbury. He stood for Parliament in 1905 and 1908 with the Political Labour League before spending four years in Britain as a socialist propagandist. Arrested for anti-conscription activism during WWI, Thorn married Margaret Anderson in 1917 and spent the 1920s as editor of the Maoriland Worker and Labour Party official. He finally won parliamentary election in 1935 as member for Thames, serving 11 years with particular interest in collective security and the United Nations. After losing his seat in 1946, he served as High Commissioner to Canada and participated in drafting the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948. He died in 1956.
